title: Melissa Barrera Says She Would Return to ‘Scream’ Franchise If the Rights ‘Were Ever to Leave’ Spyglass: ‘I Had an Amazing Time Making Those Movies’
description: Despite being fired from the “Scream” franchise in 2023, Melissa Barrera has made it clear that her real issue is with Spyglass Media Group, not the
body:
Despite being fired from the “Scream” franchise in 2023, Melissa Barrera has made it clear that her real issue is with Spyglass Media Group, not the films themselves. 

	When asked if she’d ever return for a future “Scream” film during a recent JustWatch interview, the actress responded, “not with the company that currently holds the rights.” (Spyglass is a co-producer and the current rights holder.)


	“I love the franchise,” she continued. “I had an amazing time making those movies. But a lot of the hate and the difficulty that I’ve faced in the last years is because the leadership of that company made it a point to label me something that I’m not, and they never apologized, even when I was proven right.”
	

	Barrera’s comments pertain to the company’s claim that she was acting antisemitically when she shared social media posts criticizing Israel amid the war in Gaza. At the time, Spyglass had said that it had “zero tolerance for antisemitism or the incitement of hate in any form, including false references to genocide, ethnic cleansing, Holocaust distortion or anything that flagrantly crosses the line into hate speech.”

	Barrera continued, “Even with an apology, I wouldn’t go back to work with them. So, not that I’m holding my breath. I don’t think they have that ability. But if the franchise were ever to leave those hands and go into hands that I think honor Wes Craven’s legacy more, I think yeah.”

	The “In the Heights” actress had starred in 2022’s “Scream” and that year’s “Scream VI” before she was ousted from the franchise. “Scream 7” was released earlier this year. Recently, she spoke about how “beautiful” she found the support around Macklemore to be following his removal from Ed Sheeran’s tour for his support of Palestine.
	

	“It was so beautiful to see Finneas and the band and all the opening acts pulling out in support of Macklemore,” the actress said (via AP). “It made me emotional. You know, I didn’t get that when it happened to me. I didn’t have any of that happen. It was too soon. People were too scared. But it’s good to see that almost three years later, at least things have changed.”

schema.headline: Melissa Barrera Says She Would Return to ‘Scream’ Franchise If the Rights ‘Were Ever to Leave’ Spyglass: ‘I Had an Amazing Time Making Those Movies’

title: ‘Paper Tiger’ Director James Gray Says He Doesn’t ‘Want to Preach’ Politics To Audiences: ‘Art Is Not Sunday School’
description: “Paper Tiger” director James Gray says he doesn’t “want to preach” about politics while making the festival rounds for his latest film, starring Ada
body:
“Paper Tiger” director James Gray says he doesn’t “want to preach” about politics while making the festival rounds for his latest film, starring Adam Driver, Scarlett Johansson and Miles Teller.

	“All movies are political in one way or another, but I like movies that exist with subtext,” Gray told Variety at the film’s New York Film Festival premiere Friday. “I don’t want to preach to you. That’s a polemic. That’s for debate class. The reason we can watch some of those beautiful Hollywood movies from 1940 and still find them moving is because they weren’t trying to teach us a lesson. Not Sunday school. Art is not Sunday school.”
	

	Yet “Paper Tiger” has taken on a few unexpected political parallels. Dating back to the Ming Dynasty, the Chinese used the term paper tiger to describe someone who appears powerful and intimidating but ultimately poses little threat. President Donald J. Trump has repeatedly invoked the term when discussing Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.


	“Russia has been fighting aimlessly for three and a half years a War that should have taken a Real Military Power less than a week to win,” Trump wrote on Truth Social a year ago this week. “This is not distinguishing Russia. In fact, it is very much making them look like ‘a paper tiger.’”

	Coincidentally, he only began doing so after filming wrapped on James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” a crime drama centered on a family being threatened by Russian mobsters.

	“It’s very weird because I wrote and made [‘Paper Tiger’] before [Trump] ever started using that term,” Gray said. “It had nothing to do with him…. It’s sort of like half frightening, weirdly flattering. I don’t know. What would you think?”
	

	From Gray’s early work on “The Yards” (which drew from his father’s work manufacturing subway parts and how the job led to him becoming entangled in illegal activity) to “Armageddon Time” (his autobiographical coming-of-age drama that played second fiddle to Steven Spielberg’s “The Fabelmans” on the 2022 awards circuit), each of his films chronicle deeply personal chapters of his life through the guise of genre.

	“Paper Tiger” was initially conceived as a sequel to “Armageddon Time,” one that would focus on his mother’s untimely battle with glioblastoma that ultimately killed her. Gray even considered bringing back Anne Hathaway and Jeremy Strong as his parents, but his experience watching his father become a convicted criminal took precedence in the story.

	Adam Driver stars in Gray’s latest film as Gary, a former police officer who ropes his younger brother Irwin (Miles Teller, not Strong) into a dicey business deal that lands them in trouble with the Russian mafia. Their predicament hijacks Irwin’s suburban family life, just as his wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson, not Hathaway) is diagnosed with a sudden illness. Gary dismisses the Russians as “paper tigers” (all talk, no bite), only to discover how badly he has underestimated them.

	The title’s irony extends beyond the Russians. Much like “Armageddon Time” explores the complexity of the American Dream, “Paper Tiger” depicts a system that appears navigable to an ordinary American family — until, that is, it swallows them whole.

	“This term was originally [popularized] by Mao Zedong in China to describe us,” Gray explains. “I always loved it because it seemed so vivid. A tiger made of paper — what is that? It’s the brittleness that’s underneath all of us no matter how tough we think we are.”

	Just hours before the “Paper Tiger” premiere in New York, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Trump was setting up a trilateral peace agreement with Russia and Ukraine. But when asked if Trump himself is a paper tiger, Gray went mute.

	“No comment,” he smirked.

schema.headline: ‘Paper Tiger’ Director James Gray Says He Doesn’t ‘Want to Preach’ Politics To Audiences: ‘Art Is Not Sunday School’

title: Hayley Kiyoko Wants to Make a Lesbian ‘Pirates of the Caribbean’: ‘Keira Knightley, But Gay’
description:
Hayley Kiyoko wants to sail the same-sex-loving high seas.

	The musician, novelist and filmmaker says her dream project is a queer take on “Pirates
body:
Hayley Kiyoko wants to sail the same-sex-loving high seas.

	The musician, novelist and filmmaker says her dream project is a queer take on “Pirates of the Caribbean.” “I would love to do a lesbian pirate show or movie — Keira Knightley, but gay,” she said. “Very gay and fantastical.”

	Kiyoko’s remarks came Thursday night during a panel at UTA in Beverly Hills titled “Saving Queer Media.” The program also included filmmakers Angela Robinson, Adam Shankman and Wash Westmoreland. Moderated by Variety’s Marc Malkin and hosted by UTA Proud, the evening served as a fundraiser for the Los Angeles-based LGBTQ+ film festival Outfest.
	

	Kiyoko made her directorial debut earlier this year with “Girls Like Girls,” a YA romance based on her novel and song of the same name. She said she tried to get the film greenlit based solely on the song, but financing didn’t come through until after she wrote the novel and it became a bestseller.


	She’s hoping to turn her second novel, “Where There’s Room for Us,” into a film as well. “It’s a period piece, which no one wants to pay for, but they will one day,” she said to cheers and applause from the audience.

	Adam Shankman, whose directorial credits include “Hairspray,” “Rock of Ages,” “Stop! That! Train!” and the upcoming Arnold Schwarzenegger and Alan Ritchson holiday action comedy “The Man With the Bag,” said his dream project is a big-screen adaptation of “Spring Awakening,” the Tony Award-winning coming-of-age rock musical set in late 19th-century Germany. 
	

	Although he doesn’t think it could ever get the go-ahead because of its intense subject matter, “where terrible things happen to these kids,” Shankman said, “I think it is such a beautiful poem and it is such a beautiful story and it lives in me in such a haunting and beautiful way. I know exactly what I would do with it, and I know exactly how I would do it. I see it completely, and I would love to make it more than any other movie. If that was my last movie, I’d be fine.”

	An off-Broadway “Spring Awakening” revival begins previews on Nov. 27 ahead of opening night on Dec. 17.



	

	



	Wash Westmoreland, the director behind Julianne Moore’s Oscar-winning work in “Still Alice” as well as the recent “Heartstopper Forever,” wants to adapt Chris Bryant’s 2020 book “The Glamour Boys: The Secret Story of the Rebels Who Fought for Britain to Defeat Hitler.”

	“It’s a true story, and it’s set in Britain in the 1930s, where being queer was career-destroying, and you’d be thrown in jail. It was absolutely illegal,” Westmoreland said. “It’s about a group of queer MPs who are very repressed and very secretive about their lives, but they go to the one place in Europe where you can have a good time and a sexy weekend, which was Berlin at the time of ‘Cabaret.’ So they went there.

	“They were drinking, dancing, just having a great time. It was a true expression of freedom,” he continued. “But they saw the rise of the Nazis, and it absolutely radicalized them to go back and stand up and demand that Britain confront Germany at the time.”



	

	



	Westmoreland called it a story about “queer war heroes” that resonates today. “It is a powerful analogy to what’s happening now, the authoritarians they need people to beat up on and guess who’s very easy to beat up on? LGBTQ people are,” he said. “It’s this vigilance of standing up for what we believe in and preventing the pushback of our rights.”

	“Professor Marsten and the Wonder Women” writer and director Angela Robinson said she’s been trying to adapt “D.E.B.S.,” her 2004 action comedy about a group of schoolgirls recruited to a secret government defense agency, as a television series. “Sometimes the stars start to align and then they don’t, but that would be really fun,” Robinson said.

title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ First Reactions Go Crazy for ‘Epic’ and ‘Jaw-Dropping’ Sequel: ‘Should Be Nominated for Best Picture’
description: Godzilla is back and better than ever as Takashi Yamazaki‘s “Godzilla Minus Zero” is earning rave first reactions after its New York Film Festival p
body:
Godzilla is back and better than ever as Takashi Yamazaki‘s “Godzilla Minus Zero” is earning rave first reactions after its New York Film Festival press screening. The director’s sequel to 2023’s blockbuster “Godzilla Minus One” wowed journalists with epic thrills and the first R-rated action set pieces in the long-running kaiju franchise. First reactions out of the festival are calling “Godzilla Minus One” a “jaw-dropping spectacle” and a “glorious continuation of the first film.”
	

	“A truly epic cinematic feat,” writes reporter Jonathan Sim. “It takes the King of the Monsters to a whole new level while still grounding everything in human, emotional stakes. A must-see blockbuster that truly delivers. Unmatched VFX, action, and scale. Rousing, incredible filmmaking.”


	“Takashi Yamazaki’s made a worthy successor to ‘Minus One’ with a family-centric story that’s also filled with thrilling action sequences and jaw-dropping monster battles,” adds Marissa Hill. “But it works in the quieter moments too… It’s still astonishing to me that these films, made on a fraction of the budget as current day blockbusters, look this good… the King of Monsters has never looked or sounded this grand.”

	Film critic Edward Douglas was “completely blown away” by the sequel, while fellow critic Brandon Lewis called the movie an “overwhelming achievement of kaiju filmmaking. Aside from the jaw-dropping spectacle, Takashi Yamazaki packs in an emotional wallop.”

	“Godzilla Minus Zero” is the 38th film in the “Godzilla” franchise and the 34th produced by Toho, the Japanese entertainment company that originally created the franchise. Yamazaki returns to the director’s chair after the immense success of “Godzilla Minus One,” which earned $116 million worldwide, making it the highest-grossing Japanese “Godzilla” film of all time. “Minus One” also won the Oscar for best visual effects. The sequel stars Kamiki Ryunosuke and Hamabe Minami and marks the first time a Japanese feature has been shot for Imax screens.
	

	Per the official description, “Godzilla Minus Zero” picks up in 1949, “two years after the tumultuous events of ‘Godzilla Minus One,’ and continues the story of the Shikishima family as they face an all-new calamity.” The rampage-causing Godzilla is bigger than ever this time and heads to New York City for a global action epic. 

	“Godzilla Minus Zero” opens in U.S. theaters Nov. 6, three days after it begins rolling out in Japan. Check out more first reactions in the posts below.

title: Sylvester Stallone Says He ‘Became Bulimic’ After Transforming for ‘Rocky’ and Opens Up About the ‘Terrible Toll’ of Steroid Use: It Was An ‘Obsessive Body-Worship Kind of Thing’
description: Sylvester Stallone is opening up about the less glamorous side of fame, revealing that he’s struggled with a tumultuous relationship with his body e
body:
Sylvester Stallone is opening up about the less glamorous side of fame, revealing that he’s struggled with a tumultuous relationship with his body ever since he physically transformed to play the titular boxer in “Rocky.”

	In a recent interview with The New York Times, the famed actor delved into his “intimate” relationship with his body and how it’s changed over time. “It was my armor. I looked at Rocky: very smooth, very normal-looking guy. And then I said, I think the character would start to become a bit more vain. And then in ‘Rambo,’ you’re playing a warrior, so you’d be a little bit more animalistic. You wouldn’t be so smooth,” he said. “So I started to think: Design your body like a jaguar, a cat. Not big like Arnold, but more feral and aggressive and very limber and athletic.”
	

	However, Stallone admitted that this type of thinking “became an obsession.” “It got to the point where I became bulimic,” he said. “I got down to 2.6 percent body fat when I was doing ‘Rocky III,’ and I couldn’t hold anything down. Or I didn’t want to keep it down because I became so obsessed with staying at that point of fitness, literally an obsessive body-worship kind of thing.”


	Steroids played a role, also, he continued: “Nobody does it without additives and drugs, period. I don’t care what they say. It isn’t as though you’re a junkie, but if you’re going to work out and try to stay in shape for six months straight, and you’re eating yogurt and pudding, it’s not happening.” He noted that he’d use the drugs “in a sensitive way — six weeks on, six weeks off.” “People go, ‘Oh, you don’t get that way naturally.’ No, you don’t. But that also took a terrible toll.” 
	

	“It wasn’t until I did ‘Cop Land,’ when I had to play the weakest guy in the room — partially deaf, overweight — that I felt somewhat liberated,” he said. “But yeah, I’ve abused my body.”

	Today, Stallone said he no longer sees his body as his armor, but treating it in the “masochistic” ways he did came “at a terrible price.” “If I could do it over again, I would say, ‘Let someone else carry the banner and don’t do your own stunts,’” he said.

	Stallone’s forthcoming memoir, “The Steps,” is available on Sept. 29.

schema.headline: Sylvester Stallone Says He ‘Became Bulimic’ After Transforming for ‘Rocky’ and Opens Up About the ‘Terrible Toll’ of Steroid Use: It Was An ‘Obsessive Body-Worship Kind of Thing’

title: How To Watch Neil Young, Willie Nelson, Dave Matthews Band and More Perform Live at CNN’s ‘Farm Aid Music Festival’

	CNN has p
body:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Variety may receive an affiliate commission.

	CNN has partnered with Farm Aid for a second year to bring audiences the Farm Aid 2026: Music Festival Live on Saturday, Sept. 26.

	Audiences can watch the annual music festival, which will air live on Saturday, Sept. 26 from 7 p.m. ET to 11 p.m. ET on CNN. Cable-cutters can also stream the fest live online through a variety of live TV streamers such as DirecTV (which offers a 5-day free trial) and Sling TV.


	CNN’s airing of the evening will include performances by Farm Aid board member artists including Willie Nelson and Family, Neil Young and the Chrome Hearts, John Mellencamp, Dave Matthews with Tim Reynolds, Margo Price and Nathaniel Rateliff.


	CNN is the festival’s exclusive broadcast partner. Last year’s broadcast of the festival’s 40th anniversary reached 3.88 million people globally, and CNN audiences contributed more than $615,000 to Farm Aid.

	CNN anchors John Berman and Laura Coates will co-anchor the special coverage from the Veterans United Home Loans Amphitheater in Virginia Beach, Virginia. CNN chief climate correspondent Bill Weir will provide on-the-ground reporting from the celebration of music and family farmers.

	Farm Aid 2026: Music Festival Live was founded in 1985 by Willie Nelson, Neil Young and John Mellencamp. The goal of the event is to raise funds to support programs that help farmers thrive and take action to change the dominant system of industrial agriculture and promote food from family farms. The organization has raised more than $85 million since its inception.

	Stream the 2026 Farm Aid Music Festival live online here.

title: Reba McEntire Says She Missed a Call from Dolly Parton Before Her Death and ‘Couldn’t’ Get Back in Touch: ‘I’ll Never Know Why She Called’
description:
Reba McEntire revealed her longtime friend Dolly Parton tried to get in touch with her just before she died.

	The country singer and actress shared
body:
Reba McEntire revealed her longtime friend Dolly Parton tried to get in touch with her just before she died.

	The country singer and actress shared that she missed a call from Parton, who died Aug. 25 after a “brief battle” with cancer, and was unable to get in touch with her one final time.

	“She did call me the last of July, and I was in a meeting and I missed her call,” McEntire told Entertainment Tonight. “I tried to get back in touch with her and I couldn’t, never made a connection. And then when my buddy called me and said, ‘Dolly’s gone,’ I thought, ‘I’ll never know why she called me.’”
	

	McEntire added, “I’ll find out one day.”

	The friends collaborated on several projects together, including their cover of “Does He Love You” for McEntire’s album in 2021 and co-hosting the 2019 CMA awards. McEntire recently performed a tribute for Parton at the Emmys with an emotional cover of “Appalachian Memories” and was one of the many people who honored Parton online after the news of her passing.

	“Well, I just got the news that my buddy Dolly passed onto the higher and greater side. Dolly, thank you for all the wonderful things you did for us here on earth,” McEntire wrote on X. Your love, your music and you gave so much with your huge huge heart. There will never ever be another you. We will remember and cherish every memory and every note you ever played and sang.”

	She added, “Thank you, Lord, for Dolly. She’s gonna have a blast in heaven singing all her favorite songs with all her family and friends who have gone on before her. I’ll never forget the first time I met you and I’ll never forget our last conversation. I hold it with love in my heart. I will always love you, Reba.”

schema.headline: Reba McEntire Says She Missed a Call from Dolly Parton Before Her Death and ‘Couldn’t’ Get Back in Touch: ‘I’ll Never Know Why She Called’

title: Nine Takeaways From Helsinki’s Finnish Film Affair, From Buzzy Titles to Hollywood Whisperers
description: Genre thrills and chills dominated the 15th Finnish Film Affair that closed last night, and splattered across various sections of Helsinki’s Love &
body:
Genre thrills and chills dominated the 15th Finnish Film Affair that closed last night, and splattered across various sections of Helsinki’s Love & Anarchy Film Festival and panel sessions.

	The tone was set with the opening film “Nightborn” by local genre wiz Hanna Bergholm, the inaugural Nordic Genre Lab, and yesterday’s panels about Nordic genre’s market value and positioning, followed by XYZ Films’ masterclass about the morphing of Tommy Wirkola’s “The Trip” into Hollywood’s “Over Your Dead Body.”
	

	“Genre films and series are definitely on the rise, including in Finland where we do have a history of dark, quirky noirs,” said FFA honcho Lydia Taylerson. “When Claire Willats [Two Magpies Entertainment, former Netflix executive] and Laura Laaksonen [Finnish producer, PR expert] approached us with the idea to create a Nordic Genre Lab and use the FFA as a hub, it felt like perfect timing as we wanted to replace Love & Anarchy’s ‘weird’ section, which was a bit vague as a concept,” she said.


	But Nordic fare across all genres – from body horror to kids comedy, dramas and documentaries, showcased at Thursday’s pitch day, played out strongly in Helsinki, based on the positive feedback from industry players such as Mike Runagall, managing director of London-based Altitude Film Sales, who said: “I came eight years ago for a panel. But I now feel that someone from my company should come every year. It’s a real creative hub here,” said the senior sales executive, who plans to track a handful of genre projects.

	Searchlight’s Sydney Brumfield, who was in Helsinki for her Nordic Genre Lab juror duty, concurred. “Finnish Film Affair organizers did an excellent job in selecting the projects because the quality was amazing,” she said.
	

	At last night’s FFA closing speech, Pauliina Ståhlberg, head of the festival thanked all participants, mentors of the training programs Nordic Flair and Nordic Genre Lab, and experts who sat on the 12 panels. “The panels have been great! I’ve learned about what an ‘above-the-line liaison’ does, and why producers should hold on to IP and remake rights. We’ve seen so many different genres. We all need different content at different times of our lives. So let’s help each other tell different stories, about different cultures. At Love and Anarchy, we do believe that with film and TV, with love and anarchy we can make the world a better place,” she said.

	Here is how FFA unrolled in nine takeaways.

	Numbers

	A record 630 attendees signed up for FFA, and 220 meetings between 45 different people were facilitated. At the festival, 121 shorts and 136 films from 80 countries played across the festival’s 20 plus sections. Attendance reached 50,000.

	New boss in town

	On Wednesday Stuba Nikula, the new CEO of the Finnish Film Foundation took the stage and kickstarted the panel sessions. He also sat with Variety and shared good news. On Tuesday, the Finnish government submitted its 2027 budget to Parliament and funding for the local industry via the Finnish Film Foundation should remain stable at €23 million ($26.2 million) a year, he said. Second piece of good news: the industry should soon benefit from much needed extra coin, via the implementation of the EU’s AVMS Directive. Once the law is passed “hopefully within a month,” said Nikula, the money collected from payment obligations for streaming services, set to generate between €3.5 million to €7 million ($4 million to $8 million), will be collected in 2027 and funnelled into the industry in 2028.

	Any lesson from Norway?

	Finns often look with envy at Norway, a country of equal population size as Finland where film support is threefold and funding is matched by regional and equity investors. Yes, the country has a good funding system on a national and regional level, said the Norwegian Film Institute’s rep Kjetil Omberg at a panel. That said, across the Nordics, “public funding is decreasing, deferrals from producers and partners in post is going up, while actual private money is not flowing,” he said, estimating equity funding at only 1% of overall investment in film across the EU. It’s the industry business model based on single project production in the Nordics that needs to change. “People run from one project to the next but don’t build,” he said, urging indie producers to “be more responsible.” “We have to look at the type of stories we make, who sees them. Because it’s also about who is being reached and how. The audience is key.”
	

	What’s up with EU funding?

	The EU’s 35-year-old Media Program comes to an end and audiovisual support will be combined in 2027 with spending for culture, media and civil society under the mega-Agora EU umbrella. It’s now that the industry has to come together and lobby to protect our film infrastructure, urged panellists Hugo Rosak (head of industry at Karlovy Vary) and Julie-Jeanne Regnault (European Producers Club). “Through our training programs, festivals, we contribute to the circulation of films. We do have a solid infrastructure, an eco-system that works, even if sometimes we’re not so good at flagging our success. We need to stick together and make sure the next EU program will be industry-specific to carry the goals and values of EU cinema,” said Rosak.

	Lessons from Hollywood

	How can indie producers make their IP -and coin – go further? At a panel about global franchises moderated by Variety’s Marta Balaga, experts Danny Cannon (“CSI” franchise, “Gotham”), U.K. director/producer, and U.S.-born Jodi Hildebrand (“Marvel,” “Condé Nast”) shared some tips. To make sure viewers keep watching, do create top-tier pilots or first films within franchises, as this is the world in which stories live and where characters eventually go back to, recommended Cannon and Hildebrand. Also, “don’t hold back when you make a pilot – use everything you have, as you never know if you will get other seasons,” said Cannon, who was also in Helsinki to prepare for the Mediawan Nordic noir series “The Faithful Reader,” based on Finnish author Max Seeck’s novels, which he will direct and executive produce.

	Lessons from genre heavyweights

	In today’s shifting market and “new normal” post-COVID, you need to build [your business model] on the floor, not the ceiling, and the new baseline is not theatrical, the transactional window, but ‘Pay1’ i.e. streamers, broadcasters, cable TV where consumers pay for content, said genre expert Todd Brown, former XYZ Films head of acquisitions at a panel. “We’ve been told in film that theatrical, box office is the basis for our economics, but this is a complete utter lie,” he claimed, urging producers to follow the money, where the audience is today – especially Gen Z-online. With SVODs becoming AVODs, we’re reverting to the old broadcast model, so do keep the audience engaged as this is what drives ads,” he said.
	

	Producer Camille Gatin (“The Girl With All the Gifts”) advised producers to stay away from deferments and for genre filmmakers to also think of female audiences. “Women are the ones deciding to go to the movies and they love horror, especially young adults.”

	“Nightborn” helmer Hanna Bergholm praised the co-production model, while Roar Uthaug (“Troll”) said having made blockbuster genre movies in the Norwegian language (“The Wave”) helped open the doors to Hollywood.

	Hit screenings: “Nightborn,” “The Secret Reading Club of Kaboul”

	On the heels of their international festival success, Hanna Bergholm’s horror “Nightborn” and Elina Hirvonen and Shakiba Adil’s documentary “The Secret Reading Club of Kabul” were clear standout titles at Love & Anarchy, ahead of their domestic release. Both scooped Best Nordic Film and Impact Film at Tuesday’s FFA’s preamble, the Freya Nordic film and TV awards and equally wooed Love & Anarchy audiences. At the festival’s official screening attended by Adil and Hirvonen, the documentary about Afghan women received a standing ovation and “there was not a dry eye in the audience,” noted festival chief Ståhlberg. The Finnish-Norwegian documentary has launched a pre-Oscar crowdfunding campaign.

	Ilja Rautsi at the right place

	Back from Austin’s Fantastic film where his “Red Snow” dark comedy world premiered, Ilja Rautsi who also wrote Hanna Bergholm’s “Hatching” and “Nightborn,” said jokingly: “I’m living like in a Monty Python sketch where Michael Palin plays the father who is a playwright and complains to his coal-mining son about attending gala events, saying, you don’t know what real work it!”

	About the genre pics wave, he said, “In Finland we have a history of realistic films and fantasy films for kids. In the past 15 years it’s evolved. I’m proud to be part of this change. I’ve I always loved to use fantasy, horror, sci-fi, genre elements to tell character-driven stories in a gripping way, so I’m in the right time at the right place. It’s a great feeling.”

	Buzz titles

	Among the 38 films and series pitched, besides the FFA winners, standout titles included the Finnish comedy in post-production “The Campers,” Nordic Genre Lab offers “Tick Fever,” “Linden Lane 6,” “Alma,” “Echo Chamber,” “Trespassers” and “Whistler.” Among docs, hot projects were “Mariana’s Lament” and Virpi Suutari’s anticipated “Lonesome Land.”
	

	At the festival, the most popular screenings were “The Samurai and the Prisoner,” “La Bola Negra,” “The History of Concrete,” “The Devils,” “Minotaur,” “Erupcja,” “Arrested Memory,” “No Good Men,” “KitKatClub – Kinks of Berlin” and “Jim Queen.”

schema.headline: Nine Takeaways From Helsinki’s Finnish Film Affair, From Buzzy Titles to Hollywood Whisperers

title: Box Office: ‘Avengers: Endgame Encore’ Leads With $11.2 Million on Friday as A24’s ‘Primetime’ Takes Second
description:
It might’ve been all about “Resident Evil” at the box office last week, but “Avengers: Endgame” is back on top — seven years later.

	“Avengers: End
body:
It might’ve been all about “Resident Evil” at the box office last week, but “Avengers: Endgame” is back on top — seven years later.

	“Avengers: Endgame Encore” landed at No. 1 on Friday, making $11.2 million from 3,060 North American screens. By Sunday, the Marvel juggernaut should pull in around $26 million. 

	Directed by Anthony Russo and Joe Russo, the 2019 superhero film’s re-release comes ahead of the hotly anticipated “Avengers: Doomsday,” set to open in theaters December 18. At the time of its release, “Avengers: Endgame” became the second-highest-grossing movie in box office history, with $2.799 billion worldwide. (2009’s “Avatar” currently holds the record with a $2.9 billion worldwide gross).
	

	A24’s highly anticipated “Primetime” took second place with $8.49 million from 2,874 locations. Rival estimates have the drama-thriller bringing in $20.5 million through the weekend. 


	Starring Robert Pattinson, “Primetime” chronicles Chris Hansen’s time as the host of Dateline NBC’s “To Catch a Predator.” While the film has received positive reviews and word of mouth since its debut at the Venice Film Festival earlier this month, the real-life Hansen has been less than complimentary ahead of the film’s release. After seeing the film, Hansen called it “so bizarre and so in-and-out of reality,” as well as “detached from reality.”

	Fellow newcomer “The Heart of the Beast” earned an estimated $7.45 million on Friday from 3,435 domestic locations, coming in third place at the domestic box office. The Brad Pitt-led adventure film was directed by David Ayer and stars the actor as a retired veteran who navigates a 58-mile trek to safety after he and his combat dog survive a plane crash in the Alaskan wilderness. The Paramount Pictures film is expected to gross $20 million domestically in its opening weekend.
	

	“Resident Evil” dropped to fourth place with $6.9 million across 3,684 locations. Based on Capcom’s popular horror video games, the Zach Cregger-directed film stars Austin Abrams as a medical courier who must contend with a zombie outbreak while making a delivery to Raccoon City General Hospital. “Resident Evil” earned a franchise-best debut last weekend with a cumulative $61 million, and should bring in another $23.5 million through its second weekend in theaters.

	“Forgotten Island” didn’t land quite as high as the other new releases at the box office, bringing in $4.38 million from 3,548 screens. By Sunday, Universal and DreamWorks Animation’s film should pull in a cumulative $11.5 million. 

	Directed by Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado, the animated film follows two friends as they “stumble upon a mysterious portal that transports them to the fantastical island of Nakali, packed with magical and mythological creatures they grew up hearing stories about from their Filipino families,” per the official logline. “When they discover that the memories of their entire friendship are the price for returning home, Jo and Raissa will race to find a way to leave the island before they forget each other forever.” H.E.R., Dave Franco, Lea Salonga and Jenny Slate are among the voice cast.

title: Glen Basner Says FilmNation Will Ramp Up Slate in 2027, Is Ready to ‘Raise His Fist’ for ‘I Play Rocky’ and Celebrate ‘Thoughtful’ and ‘Entertaining’ ‘Bunker’
description: CEO of FilmNation Entertainment Glen Basner was feted by “Conclave” director Edward Berger as he received this year’s Game Changer Award at the Zuri
body:
CEO of FilmNation Entertainment Glen Basner was feted by “Conclave” director Edward Berger as he received this year’s Game Changer Award at the Zurich Summit. During the hour-long talk that celebrated the accolade, the exec fondly recalled working with Berger, spoke about buzzy upcoming releases, and revealed that FilmNation will expand its slate for 2027.

	Asked about the future of his company, Basner said he woke up on Jan. 1, 2026, feeling that “the business is still challenging, but we actually think we understand it.” That sentiment was something he had not experienced since 2019, in the days before the COVID-19 pandemic. “For the first time in a while, there wasn’t this macroeconomic curveball being thrown at us.”
	

	“We are just being more ambitious by investing more and making more films,” he continued. “This year we will make four films and a television series, and next year we already have four films in pre-production and hope to make another three […] Right now it’s about maintaining the same high-quality standards.”


	As for 2026, FilmNation has a high-caliber slate of possible awards contenders, including two Zurich Film Festival titles in Florian Zeller’s “Bunker” and Peter Farrelly’s “I Play Rocky.” Basner recalled eagerly wanting to meet Zeller, having been a fan of his work both on stage and screen for years. “Meeting him, I told him to his face that he was my filmmaker crush of the moment,” he joked.

	At that point, the “The Father” helmer was courting Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz for the main role, holding steady in his belief the film would not work without them. “Because there were stars in the film, and the script was exquisite, it fell into a fairly traditional old-school pre-sales model where we pre-sold, I’d say, 75% of international.”
	

	Now, following its Venice premiere, Basner is looking forward to bringing “Bunker” to audiences, as he believes the film offers great potential for mature audiences. “This idea that people over 40, over 50, over 60 don’t want to go to movies anymore, or they haven’t come back from COVID, is the line that we hear most. We don’t believe that.”



	

									Courtesy of Blue Morning Pictures, Mod Producciones, Pathé Films
	



	“These are people at an age where they have more free time; they have the financial capability […], but we have to deliver films for that audience,” he added, saying the success of titles like “Nuremberg” has renewed his confidence in that particular audience. “I’m really excited about ‘Bunker.’ It is just a really great movie for audiences, couples in particular, to have a night out and go see something that is really entertaining, but that is really thoughtful and really has something to say.”

	As for “I Play Rocky,” Basner said the script reminded him of the great joy of watching the 1976 classic. “‘Rocky’ is one of the great movie-going experiences that many people around the world have had,” he said. “Then to read a script that talks about the making of that movie, and really the confidence that Sylvester Stallone had to bet on himself… And at a time when the news doesn’t report good stories […] the idea that an audience can go see a movie, they can be nostalgic for ‘Rocky,’ but walk out feeling inspired to bet on themselves is just great. I’m ready to stand up, raise my fist and pretend I have the same body as ‘Rocky.’”

	Recalling working with Berger on “Conclave,” Basner said the “learning curve” was getting the filmmaker’s vision on a project instead of solely going by what is on the page. “If you read the script very literally, it just sounds like a bunch of old men talking in rooms. And you would think, well, that could be a $12 million or $15 million budget. But that really wasn’t the movie that you were looking to make,” he said while in direct conversation with the director.



	

					“I Play Rocky,” courtesy of FilmNation
	



	“And I remember you talking about ‘The Parallax View’ as being a point of reference for you and talking about not just the architecture of the locations, but the architecture of how you wanted the camera to move and how the film to feel,” he went on. “What was a people-talking-in-rooms drama all of a sudden became this political thriller as we learned your vision for the movie.”
	

	When told by Berger about how filmmakers value strategic partners that are open, honest and supportive throughout sales processes that might not always be clear to creatives, Basner said, “That’s the really important part about this relationship between filmmaker, FilmNation and producer: tough conversations that include criticism, that include creative input, and tough conversations about distribution as well, and what would be the best home.”

	Basner said the filmmaking part is always “really fun,” but “once we have the film and now we’re talking about getting people to see it, that film having impact, that’s where I really feel like we have a superpower in that we just know how to work each and every territory.”

	“We’ve learned how to collaborate with the many, many great independent distributors around the world who are doing this job,” he pointed out. “It’s a unique business where everyone is in it simply because they love movies; otherwise, they find a much easier way to earn money. And you get this great collaboration; you get tremendous insights into cultural differences around the world that you get to take with you as a human being and as a professional.”

title: Mother Watched Her 4-Year-Old Daughter Being Chased By Her Father Before She Was Killed
description:

                          Mother Watched Her Daughter Chased By Her Father
body:
Double Murder-Suicide
                          Mother Watched Her Daughter Chased By Her Father Before She Was Killed
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 25, 2026
                            6:00 PM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            An Australian man was captured on camera chasing his young daughter around a house in Indonesia before killing her, his son, and himself.
      
    
            4-year-old Laura and 6-year-old Archie and their 56-year-old father, Damien John Shaw, were found dead in the southern Bali home after their mom asked a worker to check on them ... according to Australian outlets.
      
    
            The mother was reportedly out of town and got worried when she could hear her daughter crying while on the phone with Shaw before the call got cut.
      

            According to the Sydney Morning Herald, she then checked the house's CCTV camera and helplessly watched as Shaw "chased" Laura.
      
    
            The young girl was reportedly yelling "I love you, Daddy" as her father chased her. Police speculate Archie was already dead at this point.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            The Herald reports that Bali police spokesman Senior Commander Ariasandy theorized ... "It looks like he did it first to the son, and because [Laura] saw that, she was trying to escape."
      
    
            According to Perth Now, Shaw's friend said he was "struggling mentally" the last time they spoke ... and mentioned wanting to kill himself after recently losing $140K in a recent venture.
      
    
            If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. Call or text 988 or chat 988lifeline.org.

            Gottmik -- who made history on "RuPaul's Drag Race" for being the first trans man to compete on the show -- has been arrested for a DUI ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Law enforcement sources tell TMZ ... around 4:50 PM on Sept. 16, Burbank Police officers responded to a traffic collision involving a black Porsche and multiple parked vehicles.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            They add that they determined the driver of the Porsche had collided with a parked Toyota Camry, which was pushed into two additional vehicles.
      

            The insiders say 30-year-old Gottmik, whose real name is Kade Gottlieb, was the Porsche's sole occupant.
      
    
            Police say the driver, who displayed objective signs and symptoms of alcohol intoxication and was arrested for DUI. He was later released on Sept. 17.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Gottmik came in a shared third-fourth place on the 13th season of 'RPDR' ... before eventually returning for the ninth season of "RuPaul's Drag Race All Stars."
      
    
            We reached out to a rep for Gottmik ... so far, no word back.
